item.title: The Limited — Market regulation
item.description:
The Symbolic Politics of Housing
David Broockman, Christopher Elmendorf & Joshua Kalla
American Political Science Review, forthcoming

Abstract:
Voter opposition to development contributes to America's housing shortage. Prevailing explanations emphasize NIMBYism (opposition to housing nearby) and homeowners' self-interest. However, homeownership often fails to predict housing policy views, while NIMBYism offers little insight into support for policies that do not concern specific proposed housing projects -- the focus of much recent policymaking. Drawing on symbolic politics theory, we argue that voters' affect toward groups that housing policies make salient powerfully shapes their judgments about housing policies. We present evidence supporting this theory. Experiments show that affect toward developers and investors who build housing, government actors who approve it, and residents who move into it explain anti-development preferences when policies make these groups salient. Providing further causal evidence, short-form videos that manipulate affect toward developers have meaningful downstream effects on support for new development and permitting reforms. Ironically, voter dislike of the very actors who could ameliorate the housing shortage further exacerbates it.

Data Centers: Location Choice and Grid Externalities
Coly Elhai & Yixin Zhou
Harvard Working Paper, November 2026

Abstract:
Data centers already account for 5% of U.S. electricity consumption, a share that is projected to rise dramatically as new facilities come online. The electricity price and emissions effects of data center growth depend on where it occurs: data centers drive up prices more in locations with steep electricity supply curves and increase emissions more in places with carbon-intensive marginal generation. We combine a dispatch model with a model of data center location choice to quantify price and emissions effects, how geography shapes these effects, and how public policies can shift them by altering location choice. We find that data centers disproportionately locate in places with relatively flat supply curves, a pattern that has attenuated their effects on consumer electricity prices. Although single-state data center moratoria can reduce local electricity prices, they can magnify the national price and emissions impacts of data center growth by pushing facilities into locations with steeper supply curves or more carbon-intensive marginal generation.

Inclusionary Zoning and the Supply of Housing: Evidence from Boston
Gillian Meyer
University of Pennsylvania Working Paper, November 2026

Abstract:
Housing affordability has become a pressing challenge across the United States. In response, municipalities have adopted inclusionary zoning, which requires developers to provide a share of units at below-market rents. While these policies create affordable housing, they may discourage overall housing construction. I study this trade-off in Boston, which from 2000 to 2024 required buildings with 10 or more units to set aside 10 to 13 percent of units for income-eligible households. Using a bunching design, I find that almost two-thirds of developments near the threshold are instead built smaller to avoid the policy. As a result, the policy reduces market-rate construction by about 5 units for each marginal affordable unit it produces. Each affordable unit produced near the threshold provides its tenant an estimated rent discount worth $305,000 in present value, while imposing $437,000 in aggregate rent increases on nearby renters. These results illustrate the trade-off between providing discounted units to a small number of households and increasing housing costs for many more.

Strict Liability and Moral Hazard: Evidence from New York's Scaffold Law
Richard Geddes, Yeonkyeong Gina Park & Kunqi Zhang
International Review of Law and Economics, December 2026

Abstract:
New York's Scaffold Law imposes strict liability on construction employers and property owners for worker injuries that occur "at height." Negligence on the part of the worker is largely immaterial. The law, dating from the 19th century, is retained in New York State only. Other states repealed similar laws after the adoption of workers' compensation. A simple bilateral-care model of precaution in torts predicts that the Scaffold Law will create worker moral hazard. Empirical researchers have not examined the law's impact on worker safety despite its high administrative costs. We consider all-industry fatal fall rates and specialty trade fatal injury rates from 1992 to 2021 as worker safety measures. We compare New York to Illinois, which repealed its analogous Structural Work Act in 1995. We estimate that New York's Scaffold Law increased the rate of fatal falls by about two to three per 100,000 workers across industries, consistent with strict liability generating worker moral hazard. The law's high costs imply that alternative approaches to worker safety would better align workers and firms to increase workplace safety by shifting resources towards more targeted efforts to reduce injuries ex ante.

Competition in Generative AI: Evidence from Consumer Demand
Mark Egan et al.
NBER Working Paper, October 2026

Abstract:
How competitive will the market for generative AI be as it matures? Using novel transaction level credit and debit card data covering 174 million consumers and 114 billion transactions, we study the adoption of paid services and the demand-side foundations of competition in this market. As of April 2026, approximately 2.9% of U.S. consumers pay for at least one major generative AI service, with adoption highest among younger and higher-income consumers. Nearly all of these paid users subscribe to basic plans that cost $30 or less per month. Three patterns suggest limited differentiation and low switching costs. First, although multihoming is common, it has declined as providers' capabilities have expanded. Second, annual customer retention rates range from 20% to 45% across major AI providers, lower than those for many other subscription products. Third, switching rises around major model releases. Motivated by these findings, we develop and estimate a structural model of AI service demand and supply that reveals strong competitive pressure. Consumers are highly price sensitive, have much weaker preferences for particular providers than for AI overall, and view AI services as increasingly close substitutes. Our results suggest that, absent a substantial increase in AI model quality differentiation, growing substitutability among services will constrain providers' pricing power and allow consumers to capture a large share of the surplus generated by these services.

Do Stock Buybacks Cause Harm? Evidence from Financially Distressed Firms
David Ikenberry, Theo Vermaelen & Guanqun Zhou
University of Colorado Working Paper, March 2026

Abstract:
Critics argue that buybacks weaken firms and harm stakeholders. This has prompted U.S. policymakers to repeatedly consider restricting or even banning them despite a rich literature generally favorable to buybacks. This literature, though, is weak with respect to assessing harm as it generally focuses on shareholder outcomes among healthy firms and thus cannot address the broader concerns regulators harbor. We examine firms near financial distress where the adverse effects of a buyback should be most evident. Contrary to critics' claims, there is no evidence of underinvestment, excessive leverage, reduced innovation, diminished production, bankruptcy or adverse employment effects. We find no basis for regulatory intervention.

Are Prediction Markets Politically Biased?
Eric Zitzewitz
NBER Working Paper, October 2026

Abstract:
As prediction markets become more prominent, there are concerns that they will be a conduit for political bias. I analyze prediction markets returns from 1880 to 2025 and find no evidence of an overpricing of either left or right-leaning candidates, across a variety of subsamples. In recent elections, there is also no overpricing of either male or female, white or non-white, or young or old candidates. Most political prediction markets exhibit a favorite-longshot bias, and markets on near-term polling averages exhibit a very small overpricing of left-leaning outcomes (e.g., President Trump's approval falling), which is detectable only because the sample size is large. For elections, however, despite attracting participants who may not be representative of the voting population, prediction markets yield predictions without systematic bias.

Calibration, accuracy, and domain variation across one million collective forecasts from prediction platforms
Justin Dickerson et al.
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 27 October 2026

Abstract:
Using approximately one million resolved contracts and questions across four collective forecasting platforms, twelve domains, and time horizons ranging from hours to years, we evaluate the calibration and accuracy of collective forecasts in real-world settings. We found that forecast probabilities were overall highly calibrated: events assigned a probability of p% occurred approximately p% of the time. This broad pattern was evident across platforms and many domains, although fine-grained analyses revealed systematic tendencies toward over- or underestimation in highly consequential areas. While this does not mean that forecasting platforms provide certainty about individual events, our findings suggest that large-scale aggregation of judgments contains meaningful information about real-world uncertainty; when examined in aggregate, the predictions generated by the platforms provided informative estimates of event likelihood.

Rafael Berriel & Harry Cooperman
Stanford Working Paper, October 2026

Abstract:
Widely applied liquidity regulations are said to reduce systemic bank failures. Contrary to this conventional wisdom, we show that liquidity regulations reduce aggregate liquidity in stress, which leads to ambiguous effects on financial stability. While liquidity regulations increase the quantity of liquid assets held by each bank, they restrict the ability of banks to lend to one another under stress. By eliminating liquidity regulations, increasing capital requirements on illiquid assets, and placing a negative capital charge on liquid assets, regulators can implement any balance-sheet allocation that could be achieved through a combination of conventional capital and liquidity regulations. This improved form of capital regulation reduces bank failures without requiring additional bank capital. We estimate that post-Basel III capital and liquidity rules have reduced annual bank failures in a crisis by 18% relative to pre-Basel III regulations. New liquidity regulations account for about 40% of this improvement. However, the enhanced capital requirements that we model support post-Basel III balance sheets without liquidity regulations, and with an additional estimated 6% reduction in bank failures.

Pricing Power in the Mortgage Market: Evidence from GSE Fee Waivers
Neil Bhutta, Benjamin Keys & Adithya Raajkumar
NBER Working Paper, October 2026

Abstract:
Market power may arise not only from firms, but also from individual salespeople who can exploit informational advantages over consumers. The Symbolic Politics of Housing
David Broockman, Christopher Elmendorf & Joshua Kalla
American Political Science Review, forthcoming

Abstract:
Voter opposition to development contributes to America's housing shortage. Prevailing explanations emphasize NIMBYism (opposition to housing nearby) and homeowners' self-interest. However, homeownership often fails to predict housing policy views, while NIMBYism offers little insight into support for policies that do not concern specific proposed housing projects -- the focus of much recent policymaking. Drawing on symbolic politics theory, we argue that voters' affect toward groups that housing policies make salient powerfully shapes their judgments about housing policies. We present evidence supporting this theory. Experiments show that affect toward developers and investors who build housing, government actors who approve it, and residents who move into it explain anti-development preferences when policies make these groups salient. Providing further causal evidence, short-form videos that manipulate affect toward developers have meaningful downstream effects on support for new development and permitting reforms. Harvard Working Paper, November 2026

Abstract:
Data centers already account for 5% of U.S. electricity consumption, a share that is projected to rise dramatically as new facilities come online. The electricity price and emissions effects of data center growth depend on where it occurs: data centers drive up prices more in locations with steep electricity supply curves and increase emissions more in places with carbon-intensive marginal generation. We combine a dispatch model with a model of data center location choice to quantify price and emissions effects, how geography shapes these effects, and how public policies can shift them by altering location choice. We find that data centers disproportionately locate in places with relatively flat supply curves, a pattern that has attenuated their effects on consumer electricity prices. Gillian Meyer
University of Pennsylvania Working Paper, November 2026

Abstract:
Housing affordability has become a pressing challenge across the United States. Richard Geddes, Yeonkyeong Gina Park & Kunqi Zhang
International Review of Law and Economics, December 2026

Abstract:
New York's Scaffold Law imposes strict liability on construction employers and property owners for worker injuries that occur "at height." Negligence on the part of the worker is largely immaterial. The law, dating from the 19th century, is retained in New York State only. Other states repealed similar laws after the adoption of workers' compensation. A simple bilateral-care model of precaution in torts predicts that the Scaffold Law will create worker moral hazard. Abstract:

item.title: Origin Stories #2 — Human prehistory
item.description:
Tracing the spread of Celtic languages using ancient genomics
Hugh McColl et al.
Nature, forthcoming

Abstract:
Celtic languages are today restricted to Europe’s Atlantic fringes but were widely spoken across the continent during the Iron Age. How Celtic achieved this early distribution remains contested, with alternative archaeological and linguistic models proposing different homelands and dispersal routes. Here we analyse genome-wide data from 4,587 ancient individuals, focusing on Bronze and Iron Age Europe, to test the extent to which these models fit reconstructed demographic histories. We identify three main processes shaping European population structure that are relevant to the Celtic dispersal. First, the arrival of Steppe-related ancestry with Bell Beaker-associated groups after around 4400 BP (calibrated years before present or 1950 CE) across the region in which Celtic and related languages were later spoken. Second, a movement from southwestern Europe into Britain during the Bronze Age (3800–3200 BP), consistent with scenarios in which Celtic formed along the Atlantic façade. Third, a westward expansion of ancestry related to Late Bronze Age Knovíz–Urnfield-associated populations from eastern central Europe (3200–2800 BP), affecting France, the British Isles, northeastern Iberia and Italy and later associated with Iron Age Hallstatt and La Tène contexts. Although all three movements have parallels with proposed models, we argue that the final movement, from eastern central Europe, is most parsimonious for the spread of Celtic. Although human history does not necessarily follow a parsimonious trajectory and language shifts need not track genetic change, these results delimit the demographic scenarios that are plausible for the emergence of Celtic in prehistoric Europe.

Direct evidence for psychoactive cannabis use 2800 years ago
Gino Caspari et al.
Science, 5 November 2026, Pages 649-653

Abstract:
Cannabis is the world’s most-used illicit psychoactive plant, yet direct prehistoric evidence for its consumption is rare. In this study, we present the earliest direct evidence of cannabis use: offerings of plant parts and chemical compounds in ancient human hair recovered from a monumental tomb in Siberia. The findings suggest that the plant was used for its psychoactive qualities across Eurasia, where specific wild populations might have had naturally higher active compound levels. We show that the practice of cannabis consumption dates back at least 2800 years, anchoring debates around contemporary usage and informing discussions on cannabis in medicine, public health, law, and industry.

Hidden Words, Portable Holiness: Concealment and Power in the Ketef Hinnom Amulets
Jeremy Smoak
Near Eastern Archaeology, September 2026, Pages 213-221

Abstract:
The two silver amulets discovered at Ketef Hinnom provide the earliest epigraphic witnesses to a blessing otherwise known from the Hebrew Bible, yet their ritual power depended not on visibility but on concealment. Inscribed with microscopic writing and permanently rolled into tight coils, the amulets housed blessing language invoking Yahweh’s protection against hidden dangers such as snares and evil. In this article, I argue that the concealment of writing was central to the amulets’ efficacy, transforming them into miniature sacred interiors that transposed the logic of temple space onto the individual body. By embedding divine words within refined silver and sealing them from ordinary access, the amulets enacted a form of present hiddenness in which holiness was made portable yet controlled. Reading Ketef Hinnom through the lens of materiality, scale, and ritual practice illuminates how hidden texts could function as powerful agents of protection in late Iron Age Judah.

Toxicological studies on the Inca frozen mummies from volcanoes in Peru and Argentina
Dagmara Socha et al.
Antiquity, forthcoming

Abstract:
Individuals selected for the Inca capacocha ritual, sacrificed at high-altitude sites to act as messengers to the mountain deities, are occasionally found preserved as frozen mummies, providing key insights into Inca life and religious practices. Here, the authors present results of toxicological analyses of hair and nail samples from eight human sacrifices interred near volcanic peaks in Peru and Argentina. Identification of cocaine and benzoylecgonine in all hair samples, cocaethylene in two (Chuscha and Llullaillaco) and harmine in the nails of one individual (Ampato #1) indicates commonalities and differences in the ritual use of psychoactive substances across the Inca Empire.

Skills and technological innovations in the Middle Palaeolithic Levant: The Levallois approach at Givat Rabi East
Vivek Singh & Ella Assaf
Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports, November 2026

Abstract:
The Levallois method is a hallmark of Middle Palaeolithic technology, reflecting complex cognitive and technical behaviours. This study analyses the Levallois assemblage from Givat Rabi East (GRE), an open-air site in the Levant, to investigate technological adaptability and cultural transmission. Detailed analysis of cores, products, and core trimming elements reveals distinct reduction strategies and evidence of apprenticeship. The analysis reveals distinct patterns of core reduction and suggests a systematic approach to raw material use, in which knappers at GRE retained natural cortical surfaces. Despite the proximity to primary sources of high-quality flint, economic behaviours such as core retouching, artefact reuse, and minimal cortex removal were observed. These patterns highlight deliberate and recurrent raw material management, suggesting a technological tradition passed down from generation to generation at GRE. Furthermore, the presence of ‘shared cores’ points to the involvement of both expert and novice knappers. This research underscores the role of intergenerational skill acquisition in developing Levallois technology, contributing to a deeper understanding of cultural transmission processes in the Levantine Middle Palaeolithic.

item.title: Togetherness #2 — Finding and keeping a partner
item.description:
Individual, interpersonal, and socioeconomic predictors of divorce: A 12-year prospective study
Molly Smith et al.
Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, forthcoming

Abstract:
Divorce is among the most common and costly life disruptions adults may face. Maladaptive and ineffective couple communication is routinely implicated in leading models as the cause of divorce, and interventions designed to prevent divorce accordingly prioritize changes in couple interaction patterns. Yet research linking couple communication to divorce has been inconsistent, and failures of communication-based interventions highlight the need for an expanded view of early signs of risk. Alternative perspectives on divorce draw attention to the vulnerabilities individuals bring into marriage and the socioeconomic circumstances couples must navigate once married, yet the predictive power of these perspectives has never been directly compared to the behavioral model. The current analyses address this gap through a study of 368 different-sex newlywed couples who provided data on six clusters of predictors within 6 months of marriage: relationship satisfaction for each spouse, individual vulnerabilities for each spouse, couples’ adaptive behavior, and socioeconomic risk. Over the next 12 years, 39% of couples divorced. Preregistered Bayesian structural equation models and survival analyses demonstrated that each baseline risk factor independently predicted divorce in the expected direction. When all predictors were included simultaneously, only wives’ individual vulnerabilities predicted divorce. Adaptive communication behaviors attenuated the risk conferred by wives’ vulnerabilities. The best performing model explained 34% of variance in divorce, suggesting that at least one third of couples’ divorce risk is detectable early in marriage. Exploring vulnerabilities and their effects promises to deepen understanding of how relationships develop and deteriorate and can clarify boundary conditions of behavioral models of divorce.

Love at First Photo? How Platform Design Concentrates Romantic Interest on Dating Apps
Sofia Shchukina
University of Chicago Working Paper, October 2026

Abstract:
Romantic interest on swipe-based dating apps (SBDAs) is highly concentrated. This can frustrate both popular users who feel overwhelmed by a glut of attention, and less popular users who feel dejected by a lack of it. Is the concentration of interest exacerbated by the platform design of dating apps? I provide causal evidence on the effects of two common design features -- the emphasis on visual elements in profiles, and limits on the number of profiles users can express interest in -- on the concentration of interest ("likes"), and show that both, as implemented under the status quo, concentrate interest. To do so, I design, build, and run my own experimental dating app, which closely resembles conventional SBDAs and allows participants to form real matches. Across three field experiments, over 1,000 participants use the app to make over 70,000 matching decisions. Under conventional SBDA profile design, I show that visual profile components (i.e., photos and height) dominate matching decisions, and that the concentration of interest is driven mainly by users' reactions to profile visuals. Simply reducing the salience of visuals on profiles does not significantly affect which profiles receive likes, but requiring users to screen profiles on other components spreads likes more evenly (Gini coefficient decrease of 0.05 points) without reducing their number or the resultant number of matches. Finally, I show that limiting the number of profiles that users can express interest in, which many SBDAs do as part of a freemium subscription model, amplifies concentration (Gini coefficient increase of 0.1 points).

The female choice fertility paradox: A mating equilibrium shift in contracepted high-choice environments
Mads Larsen
Evolution and Human Behavior, November 2026

Abstract:
Fertility has fallen below replacement across many contemporary societies while intentions to have children remain widespread. Economic and cultural explanations identify important correlates of this decline, but they do not specify the mating-market mechanisms through which reproductive outcomes are generated. This article advances a parameter-shift model of mating equilibria in contracepted, high-choice environments, extending explanations of fertility decline from fertility preferences to the formation and timing of stable pair-bonds. Drawing on parental investment theory and sexual selection, the model locates contemporary fertility decline within a historically novel mating ecology consolidated after the 1960s. Effective contraception, expanded female autonomy, and enlarged partner markets reduced kin and institutional constraints on mate selection, allowing female choice to operate at unprecedented scale under low pregnancy probability. Larger choice sets increase comparison and can alter female partner evaluation, reducing the proportion of men judged acceptable for long-term partnership even without a generalized increase in selectivity. The result is longer mate search and a lower equilibrium probability of forming stable reproductive unions within finite fertility windows. This fertility-reducing equilibrium configuration -- termed the Female Choice Fertility Paradox -- generates testable predictions regarding union timing, assortative concentration, mediation through partnership formation, and cultural moderation.

Prevalence of Sexual Acts and Materials Provided for Financial Compensation Among Young Adults in the United States
Lara Gerassi et al.
Journal of Sex Research, forthcoming

Abstract:
Providing in-person (e.g., sex) and virtual (e.g., photos) sexual acts for pay or financial compensation (SAMP) is underreported due to stigma and substantial measurement issues. Prior research using a single item may have underestimated the prevalence and associated characteristics. This study sought to determine lifetime SAMP prevalence and associated characteristics of SAMP in a nationally representative sample in young adults (18–34 years old) in the United States. We administered a cross-sectional web-based survey through the National Opinion Research Council (N = 2,935). We used the validated, behaviorally specific, 10-item SAMP index to assess prevalence and circumstances, standardized measures of health and childhood experiences, and demographics. Over one-third (36%) of participants reported providing SAMP. Of those, 22% first provided SAMP as minors and 65.5% reported coercion. Prevalence differed by gender, sexuality, race, education, employment, income, and parenthood. Participants who provided SAMP had higher odds of depression, PTSD, problematic substance use, rape victimization, childhood adversity, discrimination, and lower social support. Findings suggest that SAMP is more common than previously assumed. Significant differences among those reporting SAMP underscore the need for harm reducing public health approaches to address health disparities, systemic social issues, diverse experiences, and SAMP’s spectrum of agency and victimization.

Maryanne Fisher
Evolution and Human Behavior, November 2026

Abstract:
The dominant account of women's intrasexual competition holds that women prefer indirect over direct aggression, a prediction supported by experimental studies drawn largely from young women in WEIRD settings competing over low or hypothetical stakes. The present analysis examines co-wife competition as a theoretically motivated high-stakes test case, using systematic analysis of the eHRAF World Cultures database. Ethnographic records from 19 cultures spanning five world regions were coded using a four-domain scheme covering causes, modes, resolution strategies, and prevention strategies, developed inductively and refined. Competition for the husband's sexual attention and general preference was the dominant cause (73.7%), followed by material resource competition (36.8%). Physical aggression between co-wives was the most frequently documented competitive mode, confirmed in 63.2% of cultures. Resolutions varied, with the most frequent being the husband's intervention or relationship dissolution (both 47.4%). The prevention domain revealed that spatial separation of wives was the most common structural response to co-wife hostility (57.9%), indicating that polygynous households are routinely organized to deter anticipated conflict. These findings support the conclusion that direct female aggression is a common, and often the dominant mode of co-wife competition under high-stakes conditions, occurring in addition to indirect strategies rather than replacing them, and running counter to the prevailing view that women rarely aggress directly.

Science, 22 October 2026, Pages 423-428

Given a brief clinical presentation, clinicians selectively acquired information to reach a diagnosis, enabling assessment of diagnostic accuracy and workup cost. René Karadakic et al.
NBER Working Paper, October 2026

Abstract:

Using 2.2 million Medicare chemotherapy episodes from 2008–2020, we instrument for subspecialist access with differential distance to cancer-type-specific subspecialists versus general oncologists. Access to a relevant subspecialist reduces three-year mortality by 4.5 percentage points (10 percent), without increasing Medicare spending or measured provider fragmentation. Subspecialists also increase the use of newer therapies and diagnosis-specific clinical trials. These findings show that specialization raises productivity when expertise is closely matched to the task.

The Price of a Cure: Luxturna and the Economic Dilemmas of Precision Medicine
Alex Tabarrok
Journal of Law, Medicine & Ethics, forthcoming

Abstract:
The $850,000 price for the gene therapy Luxturna is often framed as a story of private profiteering from publicly funded science. This paper challenges that narrative. Pharmaceuticals are a hit-driven industry: most projects fail, so the few successes must earn revenues well in excess of their own direct costs if the portfolio as a whole is to attract investment. Precision medicine intensifies this logic through two core economic challenges: (1) the “sticker shock” of one-time cures, which compress decades of value into a single payment, creating a financing problem more than a value problem; and (2) the “targeting dilemma,” in which precisely targeting drugs to smaller patient groups shrinks the market, requiring higher rewards per treated patient to maintain incentives to innovate. Rather than simply controlling prices, the paper proposes a policy toolkit that includes amortizing payments over time, bundling diagnostics with drugs and insurance, and streamlining regulation to lower development costs. The aim is to preserve innovation while expanding patient access.

An AI-native experimental laboratory for autonomous biomolecular operations
Mingyu Wu et al.
Nature, forthcoming

Abstract:
Developing artificial intelligence (AI)-native experimental laboratories for autonomous scientific exploration with minimal human intervention represents a long-standing goal. Although autonomous experimental systems are emerging, especially in chemical and materials science, they remain largely confined to domains with singular objectives, well-defined workflows and simple instrumentation. This limitation may reflect an ‘add-on’ architecture that uses AI as a task-specific tool rather than providing it with a global understanding of experiments, especially under engineering-oriented circumstances. Here we present AutoDNA, an AI-native autonomous biomolecular engineering laboratory targeting multi-objective experiments across diverse instruments. Through the co-design of models, experiments and instruments, AutoDNA realizes the co-evolution of AI and the automation system within an end-to-end multi-user framework. The system autonomously orchestrates over 20 types of instruments across more than 11,000 steps to execute core nucleic acid operations including synthesis, transcription, amplification and sequencing, while human intervention is limited to hardware maintenance tasks, such as reagent and labware replenishment. Across four representative applications, AutoDNA matched expert-optimized enzymatic DNA synthesis yields, accelerated concurrent protocol execution by 3.2-fold, completed an end-to-end DNA data storage cycle with exact recovery of the original digital content, and identified and validated a clinically detected KRAS G13D mutation. American Journal of Health Economics, forthcoming

Abstract:

Our empirical analysis leverages a unique feature of Arkansas’s Medicaid expansion, in which both Medicaid and non-Medicaid beneficiaries were enrolled in identical health exchange plans -- thereby eliminating the differences in supply-side barriers, such as lower physician acceptance rates for Medicaid plans. Using claims data from the Arkansas All-Payer Claims Database, we find that Medicaid enrollees rely more heavily on EDs for primary care even in this setting, indicating that demand-side factors alone can generate substantial differences in site-of-care choices. Our analysis identifies two key demand-side mechanisms, distinct from differences in health status and illness severity, behind this greater ED reliance: Medicaid’s exemption from ED cost-sharing and greater socioeconomic barriers to accessing primary care providers. These findings highlight the importance of addressing demand-side factors -- alongside supply-side constraints -- in efforts to reduce Medicaid enrollees' reliance on EDs for primary-care-treatable conditions.

Inpatient-Only List Removals Shifted Procedures To The Outpatient Setting And Reduced Medicare Spending

Health Affairs, November 2026, Pages 1287-1294

After removal from the inpatient-only list, most procedures shifted rapidly to the outpatient setting. For example, five years after knee arthroplasty was removed from the list, more than 75 percent of procedures were performed on an outpatient basis. Representation, Innovation, and Product Adoption

NBER Working Paper, October 2026

Abstract:

Artificial intelligence-enabled clinical phenotyping of human brown fat
Nicolás Gómez-Banoy et al.
Nature, forthcoming

Abstract:
Adipose tissue has a central role in systemic energy balance and the pathogenesis of obesity and its sequelae. In contrast to white adipose tissue, brown adipose tissue (BAT) uses energy to produce heat. Detectable BAT in humans is associated with decreased prevalence of cardiometabolic diseases. However, the complete spectrum of health conditions associated with BAT remains unknown, and high-throughput methods to quantify BAT activity in humans are lacking. Here we leveraged big data and artificial intelligence to systematically define the clinical impact of BAT in a cohort of 101,243 patients from a large cancer centre. Using a machine learning approach, we semi-automatically quantified BAT activity in approximately 8,700 patients and demonstrated that higher BAT activity, especially in the axillary depot, is associated with lower odds of cardiometabolic diseases and healthier white fat distribution. People with BAT also exhibited more favourable glycaemic parameters, lipid profiles, inflammatory markers and echocardiographic indices. Analysis of medication usage demonstrated that angiotensin receptor blocker use was positively associated with BAT presence. As proof of concept, we showed that the angiotensin receptor blocker losartan increased brown adipocyte activity and whole-body energy expenditure. Altogether, our studies harnessing artificial intelligence and big data identify new clinical phenotypes linked to BAT and serve as a platform for drug repurposing to activate this tissue in humans.

Diane Alexander, Molly Frommer & Eric Roberts

Abstract:

For primary care services not performed in academic medical centers, most SDPs raised Medicaid managed care payment levels toward Medicare rates. In contrast, SDPs for services performed at academic medical centers varied widely across states and often raised payments well above Medicare rates, placing them above the caps established by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. These patterns suggest that SDPs are being used both to bolster primary care payment and to deliver large supplemental payments to academic medical centers, underscoring a need for monitoring and policy guardrails to align SDPs with access and value in Medicaid.

Liran Einav et al.
NBER Working Paper, October 2026

Abstract:
It has been widely documented that patients in the US who are associated with disadvantaged demographics receive care at lower quality nursing homes. We find no statistically significant evidence of differential availability by race. To quantify the implications of these selective admissions practices, we embed the audit study results in a model of constrained nursing home choice. We estimate that if, counterfactually, Medicaid patients had the same choice sets as their private-pay counterparts, they would attend higher quality nursing homes on average, but the private-Medicaid gap in quality would be reduced by only 5-10%. Our results suggest that supply-side availability differences by payer are widespread, but that they are unlikely to be the primary factor behind the observed gap in quality of nursing homes attended.

item.title: Modernizing History — Economic and cultural development
item.description:
A cultural transmission explanation for the Little Divergence: The shock of the Black Death
Li Wang et al.
Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, November 2026

Abstract:
Before the Industrial Revolution, Northwestern Europe was characterized by late marriage under the European Marriage Pattern (EMP) and persistently high wages, two central features of the Little Divergence. Yet individuals following the EMP had fewer children, raising the question of how this norm could persist. We develop a cultural-transmission model to address this puzzle. Holding cultural composition fixed, higher wages raise fertility for both cultural types. Over time, however, sustained high wages increase the prevalence of the lower-fertility EMP type. This cultural-composition effect reduces average fertility and population pressure, thereby helping sustain high wages. The resulting feedback generates a weak-EMP/low-wage equilibrium and a strong-EMP/high-wage equilibrium. We further argue that regional differences in the severity of the Black Death shifted European societies between these equilibria. Regions with larger population losses experienced more persistent labor scarcity and high wages, allowing the EMP to spread and persist. The model therefore explains the joint persistence of late marriage and high wages in Northwestern Europe.

Mortality, Social Selection, and Cognitive Potential After the Black Death
Davide Piffer & Edward Dutton
Evolutionary Psychological Science, December 2026, Pages 552-559

Abstract:
Did the Black Death coincide with a change in genetic variants linked to educational attainment in Europe? We analysed educational-attainment polygenic scores in ancient European genomes. Among 4,941 individuals, the score’s trajectory became more positive after 1350 CE. The estimated change in slope was 0.046 standard deviations per century in the weighted model (population-clustered p = 0.005), although the unweighted model gave weaker evidence (p = 0.077). In a separate comparison of 754 medieval individuals, adjusted scores were higher in those dated to 1350–1599 CE than in those dated to 1000–1349 CE (difference = 0.142 SDs; p < 0.001). Higher estimated local Black Death mortality was also associated with a stronger post-1350 change in the score’s trajectory, both using numerical mortality estimates alone and when qualitative historical estimates were included (p < 0.001 in each analysis). Uneven sampling, incomplete locality matching and uncertain mortality estimates limit causal interpretation.

The Dynamics of Development in a Zero-Sum World
Augustin Bergeron et al.
NBER Working Paper, September 2026

Abstract:
This chapter examines the consequences of zero-sum environments for cultural change, innovation, and long-term economic growth. We introduce innovation into the framework developed by Bergeron et al. (forthcoming), in which zero-sum environments give rise to demotivating beliefs. Although demotivating beliefs improve static efficiency by limiting excessive competition in zero-sum environments, we show that they can also impede long-term growth. Because demotivating beliefs suppress effort, they can also reduce learning-by-doing and other production spillovers. Hence, they can inhibit innovation and act as a cultural evolutionary kludge. We apply the model to explain the cultural changes associated with Western Europe's economic rise after 1500.

Political Responses to Low Fertility Trends in Latin America: Why is There No Pronatalism in the Region?
Robin Cavagnoud et al.
Population Research and Policy Review, October 2026

Abstract:
Latin America has undergone a rapid fertility transition, with total fertility rates of 1.50 in Argentina, 1.61 in Brazil, 1.89 in Mexico, and 1.96 in Peru, levels comparable to, or lower than, those of European and Asian countries that have adopted explicit pronatalist policies. Yet no Latin American government has intervened to increase the birth rate. This article examined this paradox through a most-different systems comparative analysis of four countries during 2015–2025, drawing on policy documents, legislative records, political discourse, and official demographic data. The analysis identified four convergent mechanisms that block pronatalism across ideologically diverse regimes: the normative closure imposed by the Cairo-Montevideo reproductive rights paradigm; the institutional weakness of familist-informal welfare regimes, which lack the fiscal and administrative capacity to implement effective natalist incentives; the lasting delegitimization of demographic intervention produced by authoritarian legacies of reproductive coercion; and the structural saturation of political agendas by immediate crises that foreclose long-term demographic deliberation. We introduced the concept of “demographic silence” to distinguish the structurally produced absence of political deliberation on fertility from mere policy neglect, and proposed a continuum of non-emergence ranging from active institutional acceptance (Mexico) to constitutional subordination (Brazil), feminist reframing (Argentina), and full “demographic silence” (Peru). These findings qualify the expectation, present in part of the demographic literature, that sustained below-replacement fertility tends to generate a pronatalist response, and they offer a transferable analytical framework for understanding the non-emergence of pronatalism in Global South contexts.

Abstract:
The persistent shortage of human organs for transplantation has long been a global challenge. The prospect of substantial profit creates strong incentives for illegal organ trafficking, including murder for organ harvesting, yet empirical evidence remains scarce. This study addresses this gap by exploiting a unique quasi-natural experiment created by China’s organ policy reform. From 1984 to 2014, executed prisoners were the primary source of transplant organs in China. In 2015, the Chinese government abolished the use of organs from executed prisoners, sharply exacerbating the organ shortage. Following this policy change, the number of missing persons rose notably nationwide. Employing difference-in-differences and triple-difference strategies, we show that, compared to cases unrelated to organ trafficking (e.g., voluntary disappearances), the number and incidence of involuntary missing persons plausibly related to organ trafficking increased significantly after 2015. The effects are especially pronounced among individuals with mental illness and in regions with higher transplant demand and greater transplant capacity. Although we do not directly observe organ trafficking, the spatial, temporal, and demographic patterns we document are consistent with the hypothesis that increased organ scarcity intensified incentives for illicit organ procurement. More broadly, the findings suggest that severe organ shortages may generate unintended and highly harmful consequences, even in a low-crime setting such as China. These results underscore the importance of accounting for behavioral responses and illicit-market incentives when designing policies that restrict the supply of scarce, high-value goods such as transplant organs.

Abstract:
Between the seventh and tenth centuries, Buddhism spread from India into China, bringing with it not only religious teachings but also economic practices that were subsequently absorbed and localized. Buddhist temples in China thus became the country's earliest financial intermediaries, operating extensive lending businesses. This research traces that development through the case of Dunhuang in the ninth and tenth centuries, asking how temples first became involved in credit activities and how they organized capital, structured lending relationships, and managed risk as institutional lenders. The study draws on Dunhuang manuscripts held in the British Library, including contracts, ledgers, and temple annual reports recovered from the Mogao Caves, which together provide a rare, transaction-level record of monastic lending in practice. Three findings emerge. First, unlike other world religions, Chinese Buddhism developed doctrinal justifications for commercial lending, allowing temples to charge market rates of roughly 50% semi-annually and 100% annually without doctrinal conflict. Second, temples lent widely to peasants, officials, and merchants, earning profit margins of 20-100% that rose with borrower risk and fell as collateral quality improved, while managing risk effectively: default rates averaged 35%, well below the 55% market average. Temples also lent to one another to manage liquidity, revealing an interbank-style system of financial intermediation resembling modern banking practices. Finally, temple lending's eventual decline stemmed not from market failure but from state intervention. Together, these findings reposition Buddhist temples as sophisticated financial institutions central in premodern China.

Journal of Law and Economics, November 2026, Pages 933-973

Abstract:

Abstract:

Crossing the Design–Use Divide: How Organizations Select Innovations to Adopt
Rebecca Karp
Administrative Science Quarterly, forthcoming

Abstract:
Prior scholarship on technology and organizations has focused either on how innovations are designed or how they are used, often assuming that successful selection stems from successful design. But this assumption has limited our understanding of patterns of resistance and advocacy that can influence how and whether innovations reach organizations in the first place. To explore these patterns, this study asks, how does selection unfold within organizations, and what are the consequences of this process for the design and use of innovations? Drawing on a two-year ethnographic study, I examine how entrepreneurs piloted their AI-based innovations with potential adopting organizations. Rather than testing for learning or generalizability, organizations set up committees that engaged in process manipulation by narrowing the scope of pilots, controlling conversations, assigning pilot responsibility, and using goal claiming to align pilot outcomes with committees’ majority preferences. Committees with more adversarial members designed pilots that tested advanced aspects of entrepreneurs’ innovations, hoping for failure. Committees with a majority that championed the innovations tested basic aspects, ensuring success. While pilots run by champions mostly succeeded, these innovations faced more resistance later, during implementation, than did innovations piloted successfully by adversaries. This study shows that innovation is endogenous to selection, and reveals that champions can temper innovation, while adversaries can enable it.

The Good Idea Dilemma
Eti Einhorn, Nisan Langberg & Tsahi Versano
Journal of Accounting and Economics, forthcoming

Abstract:
Once a good idea comes to mind, it is hard to avoid wondering why no one else has already taken advantage of it. Is it because the idea is not as good as it initially appears? This concern gives rise to a dilemma over whether to pursue the idea or abandon it despite its apparent promise, a dilemma we call “the good idea dilemma”. Paradoxically, the more compelling an idea appears, the more puzzling it becomes that others have not exploited it, thereby deepening the dilemma. We study this dilemma in a continuous-time game with multiple players, analyzing idea adoption dynamics and their economic implications. The dilemma yields both under-implementation of good ideas and over-implementation of bad ideas. Its adverse consequences equally affect trivial ideas that arise frequently and creative ideas that rarely do, but intensify for ideas accessible to larger audiences or with riskier outcomes, even under risk neutrality.

Growth with New and Old Technologies
Bernardo Ribeiro
Econometrica, forthcoming

Abstract:
This paper proposes a semi-endogenous growth theory that incorporates technology vintages and the endogenous evolution of multiple technological paradigms through innovation. It provides a characterization of both balanced growth equilibrium and transitional dynamics in an environment where new technologies continuously emerge. From a positive perspective, the model rationalizes two distinct empirical patterns. Using two centuries of US patent data, I first document that the age profile of patents has a pronounced hump shape: most contemporary patents build upon technologies that are between 50 and 100 years old. Second, this age profile has remained stable throughout the past century. From a normative standpoint, the theory underscores a misallocation of research effort induced by the tendency among profit-maximizing firms to overinvest in further developing mature technologies. This yields a suboptimally slow development of emerging technologies. According to a calibrated version of the model, correcting such misallocation could generate welfare gains of 7%.

The Effects of Tipping on Workers and Firms
Dylan Balla-Elliott & Isaac Norwich
University of Chicago Working Paper, October 2026

Abstract:
Tipping is large and growing, but we know little about its consequences for workers and firms. We link point-of-sale and payroll records at 20,000 U.S. firms, which lets us observe tips from customer payment to worker earnings. We find that tips are a nearly constant share of revenue, which means hourly pay moves with revenue. Firms that begin collecting tips claw back between 23 and 33 cents of each dollar of tips through lower base wages. Tips reward effort: workers at tipping firms earn more by serving more customers. We show this with demand shocks constructed from customer spending at other businesses. A demand shock raises revenue nearly twice as much at tipping firms as at non-tipping firms, while base wages and prices do not respond. Output per hour rises more despite a larger increase in hours. Effort drives the gap because each worker is more productive, so the firm expands and recovers about a third of the tips. Yet not every firm adopts tipping: the gain is smaller where customers tip less. A model calibrated to the demand-shock estimates implies that tipping benefits workers and firms, raising job value by about half and firm profit by about 30 percent in firms where customers are prone to tip. These gains may explain why tipping has recently grown in many industries.

David Levine, Andrea Mattozzi & Salvatore Modica
International Economic Review, forthcoming

Abstract:
We present a model showing that when the demand for labor services is inelastic and individual behavior is imperfectly monitored, a firm's employees may prefer to protect its shirkers and conceal information about peers' performance from the firm.

Alice Lee-Yoon
Journal of Applied Social Psychology, forthcoming

Abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become embedded in the day-to-day work of knowledge professionals, offering substantial gains in productivity and efficiency. However, the self-evaluative emotional processes that knowledge workers experience when using AI remain underexplored. This research examines how AI use influences perceived ownership of task output and how such changes are associated with negative self-conscious emotions, including guilt, shame, and embarrassment. Across one pilot quasi-experiment, one pre-registered correlational study, and three pre-registered experiments (N = 2313) using diverse samples and task contexts, individuals who had access to an AI tool during task completion -- whether performing a standardized online task or an occupation-matched task -- reported lower task ownership (Study 1), which was associated with heightened negative self-conscious emotions (Studies 2–3). Two further preregistered experiments embedding a live AI tool in a real, incentivized work task (Studies 4a–4b) established these effects causally and showed that legitimizing AI use through endorsement did not buffer -- if anything, it deepened -- the loss of ownership. This research advances our understanding of AI in organizations by highlighting how such tool can unintentionally diminish psychological ownership and shape self-evaluative emotional experience.

Field Goal Range: How a Cultural Reference Point Distorts Performance and Decision-Making
Gonçalo Pina & Harshit Sharma
Managerial and Decision Economics, December 2026, Pages 2338-2350

Abstract:
Do professionals over-prepare salient features of their jobs? Does this distort managerial decisions? We study NFL field goal kicking, where the opponent's 35-yard line (YL35), known as ‘field goal range’, has long served as a reference point in coaching and broadcasting. Using all field goal attempts from 1999 to 2025, we find that kickers exhibited an anomalous success spike at the 35-yard line, together with a decrease at the 34-yard line (YL34). We show that this anomaly distorts managerial-decision making: on fourth down, coaches attempt field goals about 10 percentage points less often at YL35 than at YL34, even though YL35 has a higher probability of being converted, thus reducing expected points for their teams. The results indicate that professionals over-prepare salient features of their jobs with real effects on performance, and that this distorts managerial decisions.

Emma Zhao, Catherine Shea & Siyuan Li
Organization Science, forthcoming

Abstract:
As teams and team membership become more dynamic, colleagues from the same prior team increasingly transition together to a new team as a cohort: a phenomenon known as co-moving. Drawing on theories of shared team experience and team receptivity, we develop a multilevel, multi-theory, and multi-period model to examine how co-moving affects individual and team performance. We theorize that co-movers carry forward proximal shared team experience which they can leverage immediately to support their own performance relative to solo movers, who must build new working relationships. However, we also theorize that co-movers’ proximal shared team experience hinders team performance, though these detrimental effects attenuate over time. We test our theory using archival data from the National Basketball Association, supplemented by qualitative interviews with individuals involved in professional basketball. Our findings reveal that co-movers exhibit better individual performance than solo movers on their new teams and in our robustness checks we find that greater shared tenure on the prior team further enhances this advantage. At the team level, teams with co-movers perform worse than teams with solo movers, and we find partial support that this disadvantage attenuates over time. Additional analyses show that co-movers’ individual performance advantage persists over time in the new team. The findings from our interviews illuminate how these processes unfold both on and off the court. Our research contributes to the literature on shared team experience and newcomer integration by highlighting a multilevel tradeoff: while co-moving benefits individuals, it can initially undermine collective performance.
